records.title: Transient state before durable persistence
records.problem: Writing large or rapidly changing browser state directly to durable storage makes the first interaction slow and can fail at the storage boundary, taking the user's progress with it.

signals.observation: A durable write occurs for every keystroke, selection, paint, or preview update.
A write is slow, throws a quota error, or blocks the next paint.

recommendation.summary: Keep an in-memory/session draft first; persist a compact, debounced checkpoint only after the transient state is usable.
actions: Render and acknowledge the transient interaction before scheduling durable persistence.
Debounce/coalesce durable writes and retain the last known-good checkpoint.
Record persistence failures as recoverable diagnostics instead of discarding the draft.
avoid: Synchronous full-state serialization in an input or paint handler
Treating a quota failure as permission to reset the session

guard.assertion: The transient update remains available when durable persistence fails, and durable writes are coalesced.

evidence.note: A browser quota failure is retained as a concrete slow-path signal.

records.title: Build the catalog index once
records.problem: Repeatedly scanning or normalizing the same catalog during startup and navigation multiplies parse and layout work, making the whole Experience feel slow.

signals.observation: The same catalog source is fetched, parsed, or indexed more than once per session.
Changing views rebuilds an index that has not changed.

recommendation.summary: Create one immutable session index from the catalog source, then share it with views and invalidate it only when the source changes.
actions: Key the index by the source version or content identity.
Expose read-only lookup helpers to downstream views.
Measure cache hit/miss and build duration so regressions become visible.
avoid: Sorting and filtering the full source for every render

guard.assertion: A stable catalog source produces one index build per session; a changed source produces exactly one new build.

evidence.note: The sandbox inventory makes repeated catalog and launcher work a shared cross-Experience concern.

records.title: Never restart a live session
records.problem: Restarting the server or replacing the active preview while someone is working destroys the browser context and can strand unsaved progress.

signals.observation: A rebuild or source edit is observed while a live preview has active interaction state.
A tool proposes killing, restarting, or replacing the process that owns the current preview.

recommendation.summary: Keep the live server and loaded session stable; offer a separately identified newer build that the user can inspect or activate deliberately.
actions: Treat the current session as an owned context with an explicit lifecycle.
Build into a new attempt/artifact directory instead of replacing the loaded one.
Surface a newer-build notice without navigation, reload, or implicit activation.
avoid: Killing a server to pick up ordinary edits
Assuming a successful build means the new build is safe to activate

guard.assertion: A newer build does not navigate, reload, or discard the loaded artifact and owning context.

evidence.note: The control layer retains a loaded artifact while offering a newer build.
Local build attempts are retained and served through a stable preview path.

records.title: Serve the preview artifact only
records.problem: A preview that reaches back into source/build machinery at runtime couples the browser to expensive and mutable work, increasing load time and making failures look like data loss.

signals.observation: The browser requests source files, build commands, or package tooling instead of a completed preview artifact.
A served preview is not tied to a receipt or immutable output set.

recommendation.summary: Serve a completed, verified, static preview artifact; keep build and source inspection outside the runtime request path.
actions: Package once, verify the receipt, and point the preview at the resulting output.
Give each attempt a stable identity so it can be compared or activated explicitly.
Keep source/build endpoints out of the browser's normal preview path.
avoid: Replacing a loaded artifact in place
Calling a development build endpoint from an Experience

guard.assertion: Preview output is served from a packaged artifact and does not import or fetch vendor/source build paths.

evidence.note: Local Pages evidence exercises the packaged preview rather than source/build tooling in the frame.

records.title: #PROcision: assisted, exact, reversible finishing
records.problem: A tool that hides finishing behind opaque automation or scattered controls makes visual work hard to correct, verify, and trust.

signals.observation: The automatic result is shown without a direct manipulation path for precise correction.
A finishing control does not apply a predictable increment or moves verification outside the active viewport.
A correction changes durable state before the user has visually verified and explicitly committed it.

recommendation.summary: Pair an automatic first pass with direct manipulation, exact finishing increments, same-viewport verification, reversible transient state, and explicit commit.
actions: Show the automatic first pass immediately, then keep the direct manipulation path visible and unobstructed.
Use exact deterministic increments for fine adjustments; the first crop example is -10, -5, -3, -1, +1, +3, +5, +10 percentage points of selection diameter.
Keep edits transient and reversible until the user verifies the result in the same viewport and explicitly commits it.
avoid: Opaque automation with no correction path
Controls that apply hidden or variable deltas
Durable writes before visual verification and explicit commit
Tooling panels that displace the user's task

guard.assertion: The crop correction strip applies exactly its signed selection-diameter-percentage-point increments to transient state, verifies in the same viewport, and commits only explicitly.

evidence.note: #PROcision defines the professional-tool contract and the first crop correction example.
